title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Duranton and Puga’s microfoundations
text:
Duranton and Puga’s microfoundations
Gilles Duranton and Diego Puga (2004) reformulated Marshall’s trinity in precise microfoundational terms as sharing, matching, and learning, making each mechanism empirically measurable and theoretically tractable.
Sharing encompasses not only shared infrastructure and suppliers but the sharing of gains from specialisation that increasing returns make possible only at scale. When demand from clustered firms creates sufficient volume for a supplier to operate at minimum efficient scale, the supplier can charge lower prices and provide higher quality, benefits that would not exist without the cluster demand.
Matching formalises the labour market pooling benefit: thick markets generate better matches between workers’ skills and firms’ requirements, reducing the wage premium that firms must pay for scarce specialised skills and the wage penalty that workers accept for taking less-than-ideal positions. The empirical evidence on matching quality in thick labour markets is strong: metropolitan areas show higher levels of productivity even after controlling for industry composition, partly because they generate better employer-employee matches.
Learning is the most recently formalised of the three mechanisms and the most consequential for development. Agglomeration accelerates the transmission of knowledge between firms and workers through mechanisms including: spin-off entrepreneurship (employees of successful firms who start their own); labour mobility (workers carrying skills from firm to firm); social interaction (the informal knowledge circulation Marshall described); and competitive pressure (firms that can observe competitors’ practices must innovate to survive). Learning effects make clusters dynamically productive, not just statically efficient.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Lucas and human capital externalities
text:
Lucas and human capital externalities
Robert Lucas (1988) asked a deceptively simple question that connects agglomeration theory to growth theory: why does an identically educated worker earn more in a large metropolitan area than in a small town? His answer: human capital externalities. When educated, skilled people concentrate, they make each other more productive through informal learning, imitation of the best, idea confrontation, and knowledge spillovers that nobody charges for. Productivity depends not only on one’s own human capital but on the average human capital of one’s environment.
This insight has a profound implication: cities are not just sites where existing productivity manifests, they are engines of human capital accumulation and therefore of long-run growth. The concentration of talent in a location generates a learning environment that progressively raises the productivity of everyone within it. Kaldor’s Verdoorn mechanism and Lucas’s human capital externalities converge on the same point: agglomeration is dynamically self-reinforcing, and the cities that attract skilled workers become progressively more attractive to skilled workers.
For Morocco’s territorial policy, the Lucas mechanism generates a specific challenge: if the Atlantic coastal corridor has accumulated sufficient human capital density to trigger self-reinforcing productivity dynamics, dispersing economic activity to the interior without also dispersing the human capital that makes those dynamics possible will be insufficient. Infrastructure investment alone does not relocate the knowledge communities that give agglomeration its productivity premium.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Krugman’s turn: increasing returns and core-periphery
text:
Krugman’s turn: increasing returns and core-periphery
Paul Krugman’s 1991 Geography and Trade was the founding text of the new economic geography (NEG) and the work for which he received the Nobel Prize in 2008. Its intellectual achievement was demonstrating that geographic concentration, cities, industrial clusters, core-periphery structures, can emerge from symmetric geographies through purely economic mechanisms, requiring no pre-existing natural advantage.
Krugman’s model combines three ingredients: increasing returns at the firm level (larger firms produce at lower average cost), transport costs between regions (sending goods costs something), and labour mobility. From these three elements, a core-periphery equilibrium emerges endogenously. The circular causation is precise:
Firms prefer to locate in large markets, close to many customers, they save transport costs and exploit scale economies better. But markets are large where many workers and consumers are. And workers prefer to locate where many firms are, there they find employment, higher wages, and access to a larger variety of consumer goods (which raises their real income). Firms and workers seek each other. An initially small advantage in one region triggers this positive feedback: slightly more firms attract slightly more workers, whose spending deepens the market, attracting more firms. The concentration snowballs.
Krugman identifies two specific forces driving this concentration. The home market effect: a region that is slightly larger attracts more than proportionally the increasing-returns activities that want to be near a large market. The price index effect: the more producers there are in a region, the lower the price index of manufactures (fewer goods need to be transported in), which raises workers’ real wages, attracting more workers. Together these forces generate the concentration once initiated.
The critical implication is intellectual and political: if concentration can arise from symmetry through circular causation, it can in principle be initiated in any location by a sufficiently large coordinated intervention. There is no geographic inevitability, only history and its path dependencies. This gives territorial policy a theoretical foundation: place-based interventions can in principle launch the virtuous circle that concentration itself has not spontaneously generated.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Venables and vertical linkages without migration
text:
Venables and vertical linkages without migration
Anthony Venables extended the NEG framework to explain agglomeration through vertical linkages between firms rather than through worker migration, a crucial adaptation for developing countries where workers may not be geographically mobile.
If firms buy inputs from and sell outputs to each other, each wants to be near its customers (reducing output transport costs) and near its suppliers (reducing input transport costs). These linkages create a force toward agglomeration that operates even without any worker relocation. Firms in a cluster benefit from proximity to the other firms in the cluster, and this clustering is self-reinforcing: more firms in the location mean better backward and forward linkage access for every firm, attracting still more firms.
This vertical linkage mechanism is the economic engine behind Morocco’s automotive supplier cluster. Renault’s Tanger installation was itself a Midwife-state intervention. But once Renault was installed, tier-1 suppliers followed to be near their largest customer. Tier-2 suppliers followed to be near tier-1 suppliers. Logistics providers, quality service firms, and specialised recruiters followed the whole cluster. None of this required workers to migrate, it required firms to respond rationally to proximity advantages. Venables’s model describes precisely this cascade.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: The bell curve of transport costs
text:
The bell curve of transport costs
The NEG delivers a counter-intuitive result on transport costs that has direct implications for infrastructure investment. When transport costs are very high, each region must produce locally for local consumption, activity is dispersed because nothing can travel. When they are very low, location barely matters, firms can serve any market from anywhere, and dispersion can prevail because congestion costs are avoided. In the intermediate range, where transport is costly enough that proximity to markets matters, but cheap enough that trade can occur, concentration is strongest.
The bell curve: as transport costs fall from very high to intermediate levels, concentration increases. As they fall further toward zero, concentration may decrease. This means that infrastructure investment that reduces transport costs does not automatically disperse activity toward lagging regions. It may, depending on the pre-existing cost level, strengthen the already-concentrated core by improving its access to peripheral markets, the tunnel effect: the infrastructure connects without irrigating, and activity flows toward the pole rather than away from it.






Morocco’s road infrastructure and the tunnel risk



The motorway connecting Berrechid to Béni Mellal, reducing travel time to Casablanca, was welcomed as a territorial equity measure. But its first-order economic effect may be the opposite: it makes Casablanca more accessible from Béni Mellal, which could accelerate labour and commercial outflows from Béni Mellal toward the metropolitan centre. Whether the net effect is development-promoting for Béni Mellal or concentration-deepening depends on the specific transport cost context and the complementary investments made in Béni Mellal’s productive base. The NEG’s bell curve warns that the answer is not obvious, and that infrastructure investment without complementary productive investment in the lagging region may produce the opposite of its intended distributional effect.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Myrdal: backwash, spread, and circular divergence
text:
Myrdal: backwash, spread, and circular divergence
Gunnar Myrdal’s Economic Theory and Underdeveloped Regions (1957) articulated the heterodox critique of spatial equilibrium before Krugman formalised it mathematically. Myrdal’s central concept is circular cumulative causation: an initial advantage triggers a self-reinforcing spiral that deepens rather than self-correcting.
A region that attracts an industrial investment attracts workers, whose spending supports local commerce, whose taxes finance schools and roads, which attract further investment. Success breeds success. Simultaneously, a region that loses activities loses its young, sees its shops close, its public services decline, its tax base shrink, which discourages further investment. Failure breeds failure. Far from the neoclassical convergence story, where capital flows to low-wage regions, raising wages there while reducing them in the high-wage core, Myrdal observes divergence that self-perpetuates.
Myrdal distinguishes backwash effects, the processes through which the prosperous region drains the periphery of capital, talent, and youth, from spread effects, the processes through which metropolitan prosperity creates demand for peripheral products and diffuses technical knowledge. The decisive question is which dominates. For poorly integrated developing economies, Myrdal’s answer is clear: backwash systematically dominates spread. Markets left to themselves do not reduce territorial inequality; they compound it. Only deliberate public intervention can reverse the cumulative logic.
The Myrdal mechanism operates visibly in Morocco’s interior regions. Young people leave for Casablanca, Tanger, or Europe, reducing the human capital of origin regions. Their remittances finance consumption but not investment. The best local enterprises grow until they outgrow the local market, then relocate their headquarters to Casablanca. Public services, schools, hospitals, administrative capacity, are proportionally weaker where tax bases are smaller. Each of these processes, individually rational, collectively deepens the gap that no spontaneous market process corrects.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Kaldor and the productivity premium of manufacturing
text:
Kaldor and the productivity premium of manufacturing
Nicholas Kaldor’s regional economics adds the sectoral dimension to Myrdal’s territorial one. Industries differ not just in current productivity but in their accumulation dynamics: activities with increasing returns grow more productive as they expand (Verdoorn’s Law), while activities with diminishing or constant returns do not. Regions specialised in manufacturing accumulate productivity advantages over time; regions specialised in agriculture and extractive activities do not.
The implication for territorial inequality: regions that by historical accident or policy choice captured manufacturing activity experience cumulative productivity growth. Regions left with agriculture and services experience relative stagnation. The gap between them is not a snapshot of relative efficiency but an accumulating divergence, the spatial expression of the sectoral productivity differentials that Chapter 11 analysed.
For Morocco’s territorial policy, Kaldor’s insight reinforces the limitations of infrastructure-alone approaches. Building roads into agricultural interior regions without simultaneously building manufacturing activity in those regions will not generate the productivity dynamics that reduce territorial inequality sustainably. The transport infrastructure is a necessary condition for economic diversification; it is not a sufficient one.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Rodríguez-Pose: the political economy of territorial abandonment
text:
Rodríguez-Pose: the political economy of territorial abandonment
Andrés Rodríguez-Pose’s 2018 paper “The Revenge of the Places That Don’t Matter” documented a phenomenon that gave political urgency to the territorial economics literature. Systematically analysing voting patterns in Europe and the United States, he showed that the political support for Brexit, for Trump, for various European populisms, was geographically concentrated in the regions that had been “left behind” by the knowledge economy’s spatial concentration, smaller cities and rural areas that had lost manufacturing employment without acquiring the high-skill service jobs that concentrated in metropolitan centres.
The mechanism: territorial polarisation creates populations whose legitimate economic grievances, declining local employment, deteriorating public services, loss of the community identity associated with industrial employment, are not addressed by the mainstream political economy consensus focused on aggregate national efficiency. These populations eventually vote for disruptive alternatives, not because they are irrational but because their rational economic interests have been systematically excluded from the political conversation.
This mechanism is not uniquely European or American. Morocco’s political geography shows analogous patterns: the regions of the Rif, the Oriental, and interior rural areas that have been economically marginalised have demonstrated significant political discontent (the Hirak Rif movement of 2016-2017 is the most visible recent example). The territorial dimension of that discontent, the perception that investment and opportunity concentrate in the littoral while interior regions are drained, is real and empirically documented. The lesson Rodríguez-Pose draws: territorial cohesion is not only an equity issue but a national political stability and social contract issue. A country that abandons its peripheries eventually pays a political price.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: The colonial origin of the coastal concentration
text:
The colonial origin of the coastal concentration
Morocco’s macrocephaly, the concentration of economic activity on the Atlantic coast while vast interior and southern territories remain marginal, is not a natural outcome of geography. It is the accumulated result of a deliberately engineered colonial spatial economy and seventy years of path-dependent investment decisions.
The French Protectorate (1912-1956), under Lyautey’s urban planning vision, made a geographic allocation decision that shaped Morocco’s spatial economy for the century that followed: the distinction between le Maroc utile (the fertile Atlantic plains, the coast, the major cities) and le Maroc inutile (the mountains, the arid south, the pre-Saharan zones). This distinction was not a geographic description; it was a political allocation of infrastructure investment, capital, and institutional capacity. Casablanca’s port was built and systematically expanded as the export terminal for the colonial economy. The Atlantic plains were equipped with irrigation infrastructure, modern agriculture, and processing industry. The interior was left with minimal infrastructure, serving primarily as a labour reservoir and a space of administrative control.
Myrdal’s cumulative causation did the rest. Once the Atlantic coast was endowed with superior port access, road networks, industrial infrastructure, and administrative density, every subsequent investor rationally preferred it. The preference was individually rational and collectively self-reinforcing: Casablanca attracted firms because firms were there; firms were there because Casablanca attracted firms. Independence in 1956 transferred political sovereignty without reversing the spatial economy that colonialism had engineered. The post-independence state, inheriting the infrastructure and institutional framework the Protectorate had built, continued to invest disproportionately in the already-equipped littoral, rationally responding to the higher expected returns that prior investment had created there.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: The Casablanca-Tanger axis: Morocco’s economic heart
text:
The Casablanca-Tanger axis: Morocco’s economic heart
Contemporary Morocco’s economic geography is defined by the concentration of activity along two axes. The primary axis runs from Casablanca northward through Rabat, Kénitra, and Larache to Tanger, the industrial and administrative spine of the country. The secondary axis runs from Casablanca southward to El Jadida and Safi, where the phosphate-fertiliser industrial complex is concentrated.
The Grand Casablanca-Settat region alone generates approximately 33% of national GDP while hosting approximately 20% of the population, a productivity ratio that measures the cumulative advantage of concentration. Add the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra and Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceïma regions, and the Atlantic north accounts for approximately 60% of national GDP on approximately 10% of national territory. At the other end of the spectrum, Drâa-Tafilalet, Guelmim-Oued Noun, and Laâyoune-Sakia El Hamra combined generate approximately 3-4% of GDP on roughly 60% of national territory.
This extreme territorial concentration is not just an inequality of outcomes, it is a structural constraint on national development. An economy in which most of the educated population, most of the productive capital, most of the financial system, and most of the institutional capacity is concentrated in 10% of the territory is structurally fragile: vulnerable to shocks in that 10%, unable to mobilise the resources of the other 90%, and persistently generating the outmigration dynamics that deplete the periphery to feed the core.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: The advanced regionalisation and its limits
text:
The advanced regionalisation and its limits
Morocco’s 2011 Constitution and the 2015 Advanced Regionalisation law formalised an ambitious territorial governance reform: twelve regions with elected councils, substantial transferred competencies, and a Fonds de Mise à Niveau Sociale to finance social investment in lagging regions. The reform is structurally sound: effective territorial development requires governance capacity and accountability structures at the regional level, not just national agency programmes.
But structural reform does not automatically reverse cumulative causation. The reform’s effectiveness depends on whether regions have sufficient fiscal autonomy and administrative capacity to design and implement genuinely territorial economic strategies, not just execute centrally designed programmes. The current reality: regional councils have significantly expanded political legitimacy, but fiscal autonomy and administrative capacity remain limited relative to the ambition. Regional presidents lead councils with electoral mandates but often depend on national budget transfers for the majority of investment resources, limiting their ability to design territorially differentiated strategies.
Three conditions would make advanced regionalisation an effective instrument for territorial rebalancing. Fiscal decentralisation: genuine own-source revenues for regional councils (a share of VAT collected in the region, a regional property tax, user fees) would create the fiscal autonomy needed for genuine strategic choices. Administrative capacity building: the regions that most need territorial rebalancing are those with the weakest administrative capacity, an inverse relationship that national programmes must address by prioritising capability building in lagging regions. Productive investment alignment: infrastructure investment in lagging regions must be accompanied by coordinated productive investment, supplier development programmes, technical training aligned with identified industrial opportunities, and competitive financing for regional champions, to avoid the tunnel effect that roads without production can produce.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: Morocco’s urban hierarchy and its fractures
text:
Morocco’s urban hierarchy and its fractures
Morocco’s urban system follows a hierarchical pattern broadly consistent with central place theory but distorted by the colonial spatial economy and subsequent path-dependent investment choices. At the apex sits Casablanca, Africa’s third-largest financial centre and the continent’s most important industrial agglomeration west of Cairo. The secondary tier of regional metropoles (Rabat-Salé, Tanger, Marrakech, Fès, Meknès, Agadir) functions as the administrative and service centres that central place theory predicts, though their economic weight is disproportionate to their service-provision logic because Morocco’s regional economy requires these cities to compensate for the underdevelopment of intermediate urban centres.
The most analytically significant fracture in Morocco’s urban hierarchy is the relative weakness of second-tier industrial cities. Countries that have successfully industrialised broadly (Germany, Japan, South Korea, Northern Italy) typically have a dense network of medium-sized cities with specialised industrial identities, what Alfred Marshall observed in England’s industrial districts. Morocco’s interior lacks this network: cities of 200,000 to 500,000 population in the interior (Meknès, Oujda, Beni Mellal, Settat) function primarily as commercial and administrative centres with limited industrial identity.
This weakness is not geographic destiny, it is a consequence of investment patterns. The PAI’s automotive cluster development was deliberately concentrated in Tanger and Kénitra, both in the Atlantic corridor where existing infrastructure made assembly economics most compelling. A geographically distributed industrial policy, locating at least some cluster development in interior cities where land costs, congestion costs, and living costs are substantially lower, would simultaneously reduce the Atlantic coast’s congestion premium and begin building the industrial capability networks that interior cities need.

title: 19  Chapter 17 — Economic Geography: Why Place Still Matters
section: What territorial policy can and cannot do
text:
What territorial policy can and cannot do
Morocco’s advanced regionalisation law of 2015 has produced genuine political progress: twelve elected regional councils with expanded mandates, a Fonds de Mise à Niveau Sociale, and a stated ambition for differentiated territorial development. The question is whether this institutional architecture can actually reverse the cumulative causation logic that has concentrated economic activity on the coast for over a century.
Three realistic expectations. Infrastructure investment changes accessibility, not comparative advantage automatically. The National Investment Charter’s territorial incentive zones, the TNSA (premium investment incentives in underequipped provinces), and the programmes d’appui au développement territorial are necessary conditions for interior development. They are not sufficient conditions: without a coherent industrial policy that identifies specific productive activities with genuine potential in each region, and that builds the institutional capability to support those activities, infrastructure creates connectivity without development.
Education and health investment in lagging regions generates the human capital that businesses need. Sustained investment in secondary and vocational education quality in interior and mountain regions would, over a generation, create the pools of technically competent workers that attract manufacturing investment to non-coastal locations. This is the Lucasian insight applied to territorial policy: human capital density is the precondition for the agglomeration externalities that make locations attractive.
Public procurement can deliberately create demand in lagging regions. The state’s investment in infrastructure, schools, hospitals, and public services in lagging regions is not only a social equity measure, it is a source of productive demand that local enterprises can serve. Territorial preference clauses in public procurement (requiring a minimum share of contract value to be sourced from local enterprises) would channel this demand toward building local productive capacity rather than simply importing goods and services from the Atlantic corridor. This is legal under WTO rules for developing countries; it is an instrument that Morocco has used inconsistently and could use more systematically.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
text:
The Map
This chapter synthesises the book’s analytical architecture into a coherent strategic framework for Morocco’s world integration. It draws on comparative advantage theory (Chapter 11), structural transformation analytics (Chapter 11), industrial policy design (Chapter 10 and 11), balance of payments dynamics (Chapter 12), trade instruments (Chapter 11), and political economy of international order (Chapter 16) to ask a single practical question: given everything we now know, what should Morocco do?
The chapter advances in five movements. First, the GVC architecture and Morocco’s current position within it. Second, the construction of comparative advantage through industrial policy. Third, the European relationship: how to deepen without subordinating. Fourth, the African strategy: from commercial presence to developmental partnership. Fifth, the new frontier: green hydrogen, battery materials, and the energy transition as Morocco’s strategic reorientation opportunity.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The smile curve and value distribution
text:
The smile curve and value distribution
Acer founder Stan Shih introduced the “smile curve” concept in the 1990s to describe the distribution of value added across the stages of production in electronics value chains. The curve smiles upward at both ends and dips in the middle: the design and R&D stages at the upstream end and the brand, marketing, and after-sales stages at the downstream end capture high value added. The manufacturing and assembly stages in the middle capture low value added, despite often involving complex logistics and large workforces.






The car that leaves Tanger and where its value was created



A Renault Sandero assembled in Tanger leaves the port worth approximately 12,000 euros. Approximately 1,500 euros of that value was created in Morocco, assembly labour, wiring harnesses, seats, paint. The remaining 10,500 euros represents value created elsewhere: the engine (Romania), the electronics (Germany, Japan), the transmission (France), the design (Renault’s design studios in Paris and Seoul), the brand (decades of French automotive heritage). Morocco earned the trough of the smile, the assembly margin. Renault earned the ends, design, brand, technology. This is not exploitation in any morally straightforward sense; Renault took the technological risk, built the brand, invested in design. But it illustrates precisely where Morocco’s industrial policy must focus: moving from assembly to design, from implementation to conception, from the trough to the upper segments of the smile.


The smile curve framework has become more pronounced over the past two decades as global production has fragmented and trade in tasks has replaced trade in goods. Manufacturing assembly, once considered the core industrial activity, has become progressively commoditised and footloose: assembly facilities relocate to wherever labour and logistics costs are minimised. The activities that resist commoditisation and retain high value are precisely those that require concentrated, non-replicable capabilities: design competence, algorithmic systems integration, brand trust, specialised material science.
For Morocco’s GVC participation, the smile curve diagnosis is precise. In automotive, Morocco assembles at the trough: capturing wages, logistics management, and basic component manufacturing, while design, electronics integration, and brand management remain with European manufacturers and system integrators. In aerospace, Morocco machines components and assembles substructures at the trough, while aerodynamic design, certification authority, and system architecture remain with Airbus, Boeing, and Safran. In phosphates, Morocco has moved up the left side of the smile by processing rock into fertilisers, but has not yet moved to the right side (brand, market relationships, end-user agronomic advice).

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: Moving up the curve: the practical strategies
text:
Moving up the curve: the practical strategies
Three strategic pathways allow a country to move from the assembly trough toward the high-value ends of the smile curve.
Design capability development requires investing in the engineering talent and institutional infrastructure that allows Moroccan engineers to conceive, not just implement. For automotive, this means UM6P-industry co-development programmes where Moroccan engineers work alongside Renault and Stellantis design teams on components, not as service providers but as co-designers who learn and retain the intellectual property of the contribution. For aerospace, it means building local certification engineering capability, the capacity to demonstrate to EASA and FAA that a Moroccan-designed component meets airworthiness requirements. For phosphates, it means investing in soil science and crop nutrition science that allows OCP to sell tailored agronomic solutions, not commodity fertilisers.
System integration capability requires moving from executing a sub-system specification to designing the interface between sub-systems, the moment when a supplier becomes a systems engineer. In automotive terms: from manufacturing a seat assembly to designing the seating module that integrates structural, comfort, electrical, and safety functions. This requires both technical capability (mechatronics, embedded software) and relational capability (managing long-term co-development partnerships with lead customers).
Brand and market ownership requires the most difficult capability transition: building direct relationships with end users that create preferences for Moroccan-origin products independent of the multinational brand. OCP’s fertiliser brand in Africa, Attijariwafa Bank’s cross-border brand, and Royal Air Maroc’s network position are Morocco’s clearest examples. Each represents a relationship with end customers that does not depend on a European lead firm’s validation, a form of comparative advantage that compounds over time rather than remaining susceptible to relocation.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The nearshoring dividend and its conditions
text:
The nearshoring dividend and its conditions
Post-COVID supply chain reorganisation has created what analysts call the nearshoring dividend: the premium that European manufacturers pay for production proximity as they reduce their dependence on single-source, long-distance supply chains that proved fragile during pandemic disruptions. Morocco is among the principal geographic beneficiaries of this reorganisation, alongside Poland, Romania, Czechia, Tunisia, and Turkey.
The nearshoring advantage is multi-dimensional. Speed to market: for fashion textiles, automotive spare parts, and fast-moving consumer goods, Morocco’s 14-hour shipping time to European ports versus 30 days from Vietnam provides a genuine competitive advantage for short-cycle, demand-responsive production. Intellectual property protection: European manufacturers are more confident placing product designs and process specifications in Morocco under the EU Association Agreement’s regulatory framework than in some Asian locations where IP enforcement is weaker. Carbon footprint: as European supply chain decarbonation requirements intensify, proximity reduces embedded transport emissions, a qualitative competitive advantage that Morocco’s renewable energy transition will reinforce.
But the nearshoring dividend requires active capture. It does not automatically redirect investment that would otherwise go to Poland or Romania. Three conditions determine whether Morocco captures a larger nearshoring share in the coming decade. Certification and quality ecosystems: European manufacturers will not nearshore to locations where supplier quality certification (IATF, EN9100, ISO 22000) is unavailable or unreliable. Morocco’s sector-specific training infrastructure (IFMIA, IMA) and quality certification support must expand to cover the full range of sectors where nearshoring potential exists. Logistics fluency: just-in-time delivery to European clients requires not only port infrastructure but customs clearance speed, bonded warehouse networks, and cold chain integrity that Morocco is building but has not fully achieved. Language and cultural compatibility: Morocco’s French-Spanish-Arabic language profile, combined with a workforce with genuine secondary and technical education, provides a communication advantage over many competing nearshoring locations that serves both the manufacturing and the business services dimensions of European nearshoring.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The digital economy insertion
text:
The digital economy insertion
Morocco’s offshore IT and business process outsourcing (BPO) sector, approximately 120,000 direct employees in 2023, concentrated in Casablanca Nearshore, Rabat Technopolis, and Marrakech, represents the most successful services-sector insertion into the global economy since automotive. The sector’s competitive profile: French-language capability for French-speaking European markets, growing Arabic-language capability for Gulf and North African markets, competitive labour costs relative to French internal alternatives, and improving technical skills in software development, data analytics, and cloud infrastructure.
The strategic challenge for digital services is the same as for industrial production: moving from the assembly trough of the smile curve (executing defined tasks in defined formats) toward the higher-value ends (designing solutions, managing client relationships, building proprietary technology). The call centre that executes a French insurer’s customer service script is at the trough; the software engineering team that co-develops a financial technology product with a European fintech is closer to the high-value end. Morocco’s digital strategy requires deliberately building the capability infrastructure (engineering education, incubation ecosystems, intellectual property protection) that enables the transition from execution to conception.
UM6P’s engineering programmes, ENSIAS, École Polytechnique de Laâyoune, and the dozens of private higher education institutions growing in the digital skills space are the supply side of this transition. The demand side, European and Gulf firms willing to place genuine engineering work, not just execution tasks, in Morocco, requires both the supply of talent and the contractual infrastructure (IP protection, data security certification, regulatory compliance) that makes complex service offshoring viable. Casablanca Finance City’s role in providing this regulatory credibility for financial services can be replicated in digital services through appropriate certification and regulatory framework development.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: Static versus dynamic comparative advantage
text:
Static versus dynamic comparative advantage
The central distinction in development strategy is between static comparative advantage (what you are currently most efficient at, relative to other activities, given existing capabilities) and dynamic comparative advantage (what you will be most efficient at in ten to twenty years, given investment in capabilities today).
Morocco’s static comparative advantage in 2024: phosphate rock processing, assembly manufacturing (automotive, aerospace, textiles), proximity services to European clients (BPO, nearshore IT), and agricultural exports (tomatoes, citrus, olives). These are real advantages that generate real export revenues. Morocco should exploit them. But exploiting static comparative advantage while neglecting dynamic capability-building is the prescription for permanent periphery: becoming ever more efficient at activities whose value the smile curve places at the trough.
The East Asian developmental states understood this distinction operationally. Korea in 1965 had static comparative advantage in simple textiles and cheap labour. It chose to invest in steel and shipbuilding, where it had no comparative advantage at all, deliberately sacrificing short-run efficiency for long-run capability building. Within fifteen years, Korean steel and shipbuilding were globally competitive. Within thirty years, Korean electronics and semiconductors were the world frontier. The comparative advantage had been constructed, not found.
Morocco cannot replicate the Korean trajectory in detail, different historical moment, different institutional context, different international rules. But the strategic logic is transferable: identify activities where dynamic comparative advantage can be built given current capabilities and the product space adjacencies, invest in the capabilities they require, and accept the learning costs of the transition period.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The four strategic pillars
text:
The four strategic pillars
Morocco’s distinctive strategic assets, what it has that few others can replicate, define the four pillars around which dynamic comparative advantage construction makes most sense.
Pillar 1, Renewable energy endowment: exceptional solar irradiation (among the world’s highest in the southern regions), consistent Atlantic winds, and proximity to European energy demand create an energy production comparative advantage that is geographically permanent and becoming economically decisive as decarbonation progresses. This is not merely a power generation opportunity; it is the foundation for energy-intensive chemical industries (green ammonia, green hydrogen, battery cathode materials) that Morocco can produce at costs competitive with any location in the accessible-to-Europe world.
Pillar 2, Phosphate chemistry platform: the world’s largest phosphate reserves, combined with existing industrial chemistry capability at OCP’s Jorf Lasfar and Safi complexes, create a platform for diversification toward battery materials (lithium iron phosphate chemistry requires phosphoric acid as a key input), specialty agrochemicals, and food security-adjacent industrial chemistry. The phosphate platform is not simply a resource, it is an industrial chemistry base from which adjacent products can be developed.
Pillar 3, European proximity and regulatory alignment: geographic adjacency to the world’s most demanding regulatory and quality environment has generated capabilities in Moroccan industry that constitute a non-trivial asset: IATF 16949 automotive quality systems, AS9100 aerospace certification, EU phytosanitary compliance in agriculture. These certifications represent accumulated institutional knowledge that competing low-cost locations are often years away from replicating. Proximity creates a just-in-time advantage in addition to the quality advantages.
Pillar 4, African platform position: Morocco’s connectivity to sub-Saharan Africa, through Tanger Med’s container volumes, Royal Air Maroc’s network, the banking presence, and the OCP fertiliser strategy, creates a hub position that no other country combines with similar European integration. This double insertion is Morocco’s most distinctive geopolitical asset: the ability to be the commercial and logistical bridge between Europe and Africa.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: What makes a strategy different from a wish list
text:
What makes a strategy different from a wish list
A genuine strategic orientation differs from a wish list in three ways: it makes explicit trade-offs (choosing to do X means not doing Y with the same resources), it specifies implementation mechanisms (not just what but who does what, under which conditionality, evaluated by which metrics), and it has temporal coherence (the sequence of investments builds capability cumulatively rather than investing simultaneously in unrelated directions).
Morocco’s successive industrial strategies, Plan Émergence, PNEI, PAI, have been stronger on ambition than on mechanism, stronger on target-setting than on conditionality, and stronger on sectoral identification than on sequencing logic. The contribution of the analytical framework developed across this book, and particularly the four-condition framework, the product space, and the HRV growth diagnostics, is to provide the missing operational specificity: which coordination failures are being addressed, which institutional capabilities are being built, which performance milestones trigger continuation versus exit, and which adjacency steps build on each other.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The governance of FDI: from attraction to anchoring
text:
The governance of FDI: from attraction to anchoring
Morocco’s FDI governance has been primarily an attraction exercise: reducing administrative barriers, offering fiscal incentives, providing infrastructure, and marketing the country to potential investors. The transition from attraction to anchoring, ensuring that FDI generates durable productive capabilities rather than footloose assembly operations, requires a governance architecture that Morocco has not yet fully built.
The anchoring instruments are known. Local content requirements with graduated escalation: OEM investors committed to specific local content milestones (verified annually by independent auditors) have incentive to develop their local supply base rather than relying indefinitely on imports. The annual escalation creates continuous upgrading pressure. Technology co-development obligations: the most sophisticated version of anchoring requires lead firms to place genuine engineering work with Moroccan design teams, not merely manufacturing sub-contracts. This requires Moroccan engineering capacity (the supply side) and investment agreement provisions that reward knowledge transfer (the demand side). Profit reinvestment incentives: Morocco’s current fiscal framework treats all OCP, Renault, and Safran profits equivalently for taxation, whether reinvested locally or repatriated. A two-tier system, lower effective tax rates on profits reinvested in Morocco’s productive capacity than on repatriated dividends, would create a financial incentive for local reinvestment that currently operates only through general tax provisions.
The political economy challenge: lead firms that have accepted current incentive packages without performance conditions will resist retroactive conditionality. The governance architecture for anchoring must therefore be built primarily through new agreements (applying conditions to new investments and new incentive packages) while finding ways to encourage voluntary deepening by existing investors through positive rather than punitive instruments. OCP’s supply chain development programmes, working with local chemical suppliers to progressively substitute imports, and Renault’s supplier development academies are models of what voluntary anchoring can achieve when the lead firm’s own interests in local supply quality align with the policy objective.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The balance sheet of the EU association
text:
The balance sheet of the EU association
Morocco’s Association Agreement with the EU (2000) and the aspiration toward a Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (ALECA) represent the most consequential commercial policy framework in Morocco’s recent history. The honest balance sheet requires acknowledging both what the relationship has delivered and what it has cost.
What it has delivered: preferential access to the world’s most demanding market has driven the automotive and aerospace clusters beyond what domestic market demand could have generated; EU quality and regulatory standards have forced genuine quality upgrading in food exports, textiles, and industrial products; the regulatory alignment required by association has improved governance in several domains, including competition law, financial market regulation, and food safety; and the credibility signal of EU association has reduced the risk premium that investors and creditors apply to Morocco relative to comparable economies.
What it has cost: sectors unprotected by transition periods, segments of domestic food processing, textile manufacturing, experienced competitive shocks without adequate adjustment support. The asymmetry in agricultural market access (Morocco faces seasonal quotas and phytosanitary barriers on its most competitive exports) while accepting industrial goods liberalisation reflects the negotiating power differential of a large bloc facing a medium-income country. The investment protection provisions create potential constraints on future industrial policy instruments.
The ALECA strategic calculus: extending liberalisation to services, public procurement, and intellectual property would deepen regulatory alignment and potentially open large service export markets. But it would also discipline industrial policy instruments, public procurement preferences, some forms of state aid, intellectual property flexibilities, that Morocco currently uses or could use for development objectives. The Rodrik trilemma applies directly: deep integration gains market access while constraining policy sovereignty. Morocco’s negotiating objective should be asymmetric commitments that discipline regulatory quality (which improves Moroccan governance) without foreclosing the industrial policy space that Morocco needs for productive transformation.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: Rules of origin as industrial policy instrument
text:
Rules of origin as industrial policy instrument
One of the least-discussed but most consequential dimensions of Morocco’s EU trade relationship is the rules of origin in preferential trade agreements. Rules of origin determine what share of a product must be produced domestically or regionally to qualify for preferential tariff treatment. They are simultaneously a technical trade instrument and a de facto industrial policy tool.
For Morocco’s automotive sector, the EU Association Agreement’s rules of origin require a minimum regional value content for vehicles to qualify as “Moroccan” for tariff purposes. The transition to electric vehicles is tightening these rules: the EU is progressively requiring higher local content in battery and electronic systems. This tightening creates a powerful incentive for Morocco to develop local battery and electronics manufacturing, not to comply with a regulatory requirement for its own sake, but because the market access premium on being genuinely origin-compliant is substantial.
Morocco can use rules of origin negotiations strategically: pushing for rules that reward and incentivise the productive deepening investments that the industrial policy agenda requires, rather than rules that would certify superficial assembly as origin-compliant. Rules of origin are one of the few trade policy instruments that WTO disciplines leave relatively unconstrained, making them a significant space for industrial policy ambition within the EU association framework.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The AfCFTA opportunity: what it requires to be real
text:
The AfCFTA opportunity: what it requires to be real
The African Continental Free Trade Area creates, in legal architecture, the world’s largest preferential trade area. Its economic impact will be determined by implementation, infrastructure, and whether production follows trade rules in creating actual cross-border value chains rather than simply rerouting existing trade flows to capture tariff preferences.
For Morocco, the AfCFTA represents the most significant new market opportunity of the coming decade, but capturing it requires complementary investments that preferential tariff rates alone cannot provide. Payment infrastructure: the cost and difficulty of paying and collecting across African borders remains a binding constraint. The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) is a partial response; deepening it and ensuring Morocco’s banking system is fully integrated is a priority. Logistics infrastructure: despite Tanger Med’s global rank, the cost of sending a container from Casablanca to Lagos or Nairobi via sea exceeds the cost of the same container to northern Europe, a geographic reality that trans-Saharan connectivity investment partially addresses. Regulatory harmonisation: rules of origin within AfCFTA are still being negotiated; Morocco has a direct interest in rules that reward value addition within the continent and that are simple enough for SMEs to use.
Morocco’s competitive advantages in the AfCFTA context are specific and defensible: processed fertilisers with African-tailored formulations (OCP’s strategy), banking and insurance services with deep African market knowledge (Attijariwafa Bank, Saham), construction and infrastructure services (BMCE, Moroccan construction firms), agri-food processing (adapting products for African taste profiles), and pharmaceutical manufacturing (generic medicines with import substitution potential in large African markets).

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: Partnership versus extraction: the governance test
text:
Partnership versus extraction: the governance test
The distinction between productive partnership and commercial extraction in Morocco’s African engagement is not merely ethical, it is strategic. An engagement that builds genuine productive capabilities in partner countries generates the sustainable relationships that anchor Morocco’s hub position over decades. An engagement that is primarily extractive or that primarily benefits Moroccan firms at the expense of local development generates the political backlash that has affected other extraterritorial commercial actors in Africa, from Chinese infrastructure contractors to French agri-business firms.
The governance test for Morocco’s African engagement is concrete: Do Moroccan banks in West Africa primarily mobilise local savings for local productive investment, or do they primarily serve as conduits for Moroccan-origin commercial credit? Does OCP’s African fertiliser strategy primarily sell commodity fertilisers or primarily build local agronomic capability that deepens the relationship? Do Moroccan construction firms primarily employ local labour, local materials, and local subcontractors, or do they primarily replicate the Chinese infrastructure model of imported labour and materials?
Hirschman’s distinction between the teaching sector and the enclave applies at the level of cross-border economic relationships: a Moroccan banking presence in Côte d’Ivoire that primarily finances Moroccan export sales is an enclave; one that mobilises Ivorian savings, trains Ivorian bankers, and finances Ivorian SME investment is a teaching relationship. Morocco’s long-run African hub ambition is only achievable through the latter model.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: Morocco’s renewable geometry
text:
Morocco’s renewable geometry
Morocco’s potential competitive advantage in green energy production rests on a convergence of three geographic and resource factors that few other countries combine.
Solar irradiation: Morocco’s southern regions and Saharan zones receive among the world’s highest direct normal irradiance (DNI) levels, comparable to the best Atacama Desert sites in Chile. The Noor Ouarzazate complex demonstrated that concentrated solar power at scale is commercially viable in Morocco; the cost trajectory for photovoltaic systems has made even larger-scale solar development economically compelling.
Wind resources: Morocco’s Atlantic coast has consistent, strong winds that complement solar generation (wind tends to be stronger at times when solar production is lower, creating a natural baseload complementarity). The Tarfaya wind farm and the subsequent Aftissat developments demonstrated world-class capacity factors.
Proximity to demand: Morocco is 14 kilometres from Spain at the Strait of Gibraltar and approximately 2,000 kilometres from Germany, dramatically closer to European energy demand than most other premium renewable resource sites (Australian solar, Kazakhstani wind, Gulf solar). This proximity matters for two reasons: electrical interconnection is technically feasible at Morocco-Europe distances (high-voltage direct current subsea cables), and ammonia or hydrogen pipeline infrastructure is economically viable in ways that would not be true for Australia-to-Europe hydrogen export.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: Green hydrogen: the platform opportunity
text:
Green hydrogen: the platform opportunity
Green hydrogen, produced by electrolyzing water using renewable electricity, is simultaneously Morocco’s most significant new industrial development opportunity and its most complex strategic challenge. The opportunity: Morocco can produce green hydrogen at costs that will be competitive with any accessible-to-Europe production location as electrolyser costs continue falling along their documented learning curve trajectory (from approximately $1,000/kW in 2015 toward $200/kW by 2030 on current projections).
The strategic challenge: the green hydrogen industry does not yet exist at commercial scale anywhere. Morocco would be entering as a pioneer in a market where the technology is rapidly evolving, the demand signals are political as much as commercial (European REPowerEU commitments), and the infrastructure (pipelines, port terminals, shipping) requires multi-billion-dollar investments with fifteen-year construction horizons. The risk is not that green hydrogen will fail commercially, the fundamental economics are sound, but that Morocco may make the infrastructure investments on a timeline that does not match market development, or on terms that give lead firms access to the resource without adequate value capture for Morocco.
The industrial policy design for green hydrogen must therefore address simultaneously: the electrolyser cost reduction trajectory and how Morocco participates in it (domestic manufacturing ambition versus import-and-operate); the infrastructure ownership structure (public versus private versus hybrid, and which infrastructure elements Morocco must own to retain rent capture); the linkage between green hydrogen production and downstream industries (green ammonia for OCP’s fertiliser decarbonation, battery cathode materials processing) that anchor the value chain domestically; and the regulatory framework that makes long-term off-take agreements credible enough to attract private financing.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: Battery materials: the phosphate-energy convergence
text:
Battery materials: the phosphate-energy convergence
The convergence between Morocco’s phosphate endowment and the electric vehicle battery supply chain creates what may be the single most consequential strategic opportunity of the next decade. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry, used in approximately 40% of global EV battery production in 2023 and growing, uses phosphoric acid as its primary cathode material precursor. Morocco’s phosphate reserves combined with OCP’s existing phosphoric acid production infrastructure create a structural entry point into the battery materials supply chain.
The value chain from phosphate rock to LFP battery cell has multiple stages: mining, phosphoric acid production (OCP already does this at massive scale), purification to battery-grade standards (new capability investment needed), iron phosphate precursor synthesis (new chemistry investment), LFP cathode active material production, and battery cell manufacturing. Each stage adds value and requires progressively more specialised capability.
Morocco’s realistic near-term ambition: supplying battery-grade phosphoric acid and LFP precursor materials to battery manufacturers in Europe and potentially North Africa. This requires new investment in purification and synthesis chemistry, investments that UM6P’s materials science and chemistry departments are already researching. The longer-term ambition: battery cell manufacturing in Morocco, supplying the European EV industry with cells produced from Moroccan renewable energy and Moroccan phosphate chemistry, closing a circle that would place Morocco at the intersection of two of the 21st century’s defining industrial transitions.

title: 20  Chapter 18 — Strategies for World Integration: Morocco’s Choices
section: The financing of transformation: closing the investment gap
text:
The financing of transformation: closing the investment gap
Morocco’s productive transformation requires investment at a scale and over a time horizon that neither private markets nor the current public budget can individually finance. Three financing gaps require specific institutional responses that complement the industrial policy architecture.
Long-horizon industrial investment in EV components, battery materials, green hydrogen infrastructure, and aerospace capability requires patient capital with maturities of ten to twenty years. Morocco’s banking system, despite its relative development, is structurally oriented toward shorter-horizon commercial and real estate lending. The Fonds Mohammed VI pour l’Investissement, with its mandate to co-invest in transformative projects, is the institutional response, but its capitalisation and governance must be calibrated to the scale of the challenge. A 10 billion dirham fund can anchor a handful of transformative investments; fully capitalising the productive transformation that Morocco needs requires fund capitalisation an order of magnitude larger, matched by international co-financing from the EIB, AfDB, IsDB, and bilateral development finance institutions.
SME supplier development in automotive, aerospace, and agri-food requires a dedicated instrument that closes the gap between the quality standards required by international lead firms and what locally owned Moroccan SMEs currently provide. Tamwilcom’s guarantee instruments are the right design but insufficient in scale and insufficiently oriented toward technology upgrading milestones. A sectoral supplier development fund, co-financed by the state and by the anchor firms that would benefit from local sourcing deepening, would align incentives with industrial policy objectives.
Research and development co-investment between Moroccan universities (UM6P, ENSET, ENIM, ENSA network) and industrial enterprises requires funding mechanisms that bridge the gap between academic research cycles and industrial commercialisation requirements. The NMD identified this gap; the industrial research partnerships that UM6P has built with OCP and with several automotive and aerospace firms are the model that needs scaling. The fiscal instrument of a generous R&D tax credit available to firms that co-invest with Moroccan universities would simultaneously incentivise industrial research and deepen the university-industry connection that Morocco’s knowledge economy requires.
The financing architecture for transformation is therefore not primarily a problem of insufficient capital, Morocco’s banking system is liquid and the state has maintained fiscal credibility. It is a problem of patient, risk-sharing, mission-oriented capital that conventional banking does not provide and that Morocco’s public development finance institutions are not yet fully equipped to deliver at the required scale.

title: 21  Chapter 19 — Hegemonic Cycles and the Long Run: A Concluding Essay
text:
Prologue: The Question that Every Chapter Approached
Throughout this book, a question has been circling just beneath the surface of every chapter’s technical analysis. In Chapter 3, when we asked why some firms grow while others stagnate, the deeper question was about the institutional conditions under which productive investment becomes rational. In Chapter 8, when we traced the anatomy of financial crises from Minsky’s endogenous instability to Fisher’s debt deflation spiral, the deeper question was about the relationship between financial accumulation and productive investment, and why capitalism repeatedly substitutes the former for the latter. In Chapter 10, when we diagnosed Morocco’s assembly paradox, the deeper question was about who captures value from industrial activity and why the distribution persistently favours those with technological leverage over those with labour and natural resources. In Chapter 12, when we traced the asymmetry between the dollar’s “exorbitant privilege” and Morocco’s “original sin” of foreign-currency debt, the deeper question was about the political architecture of the international monetary system and whose interests it serves.
That recurring deeper question is the subject of this chapter. It asks: what structural forces, operating at timescales longer than any policy cycle, determine the constraints within which Morocco’s economic choices are made? And what does a long-run reading of those forces suggest about the possibilities available to Morocco in the coming decades?

title: 21  Chapter 19 — Hegemonic Cycles and the Long Run: A Concluding Essay
section: Why economists need Braudel
text:
Why economists need Braudel
Economic analysis, as practised in the mainstream tradition, operates primarily in the short run. Quarterly GDP figures, monthly inflation readings, annual budget balances: the temporal horizon of most policy analysis is one to five years. This is rational given the incentive structures facing economists and policymakers, elections happen every four years, bond markets react to next quarter’s current account, but it systematically misses the structural forces that operate on longer timescales and that ultimately determine whether short-run policies achieve their objectives.
Fernand Braudel’s contribution to economic thinking was methodological: he insisted that historical reality operates simultaneously at three temporal registers that require different analytical instruments and reveal different truths.
The longue durée (centuries-long duration) is the domain of geographic and structural constraints that change so slowly they appear almost fixed within a human lifetime. Morocco’s Atlantic and Mediterranean geography, its position at the intersection of European, African, and Arab-Islamic civilisational zones, its control of the Gibraltar approach, its exceptional solar and wind resources, is a longue durée reality. No policy created it; no single policy can eliminate it. It is the geological and climatic foundation on which Morocco’s economic possibilities are built. A development strategy that ignores the longue durée may be technically coherent while being fundamentally misconceived: investing in activities that fight the structural geography rather than leveraging it.
The conjuncture (decade-to-generation duration) is the domain of economic cycles, institutional regimes, and technological paradigms. The current conjuncture includes: the energy transition (a thirty-year restructuring of global energy systems that is reshaping comparative advantages); the demographic dividend (Morocco’s young population, an asset if education and employment are adequate, a liability if they are not); the hegemonic transition from American unipolarity toward multipolarity; and the digital production revolution that is progressively automating the assembly activities on which Morocco’s industrial base currently rests. These conjunctural forces cannot be individually controlled, but they can be anticipated, and strategic choices can be designed to ride their momentum rather than resist it.
The événement (months-to-years duration) is the domain of political decisions, natural disasters, and financial shocks. The COVID pandemic, the Ukraine war’s food price transmission, the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake: these events are consequential and demand policy responses. But they do not alter Morocco’s longue durée geographic assets or its conjunctural positioning. A government that exhausts its analytical energy on event-level responses without building the structural capabilities that conjunctural windows demand is consuming its capital without investing it.
The implication of this tripartite temporal architecture for Morocco’s strategic analysis: the most important policy choices are those that align with the conjuncture’s momentum while building on the longue durée advantages. Green hydrogen investment aligns with the energy transition conjuncture while building on Morocco’s solar and wind longue durée. Battery materials investment aligns with the EV conjuncture while building on the phosphate longue durée. Neither is possible without the institutional and industrial capability investments that the preceding chapters have analysed.

title: 21  Chapter 19 — Hegemonic Cycles and the Long Run: A Concluding Essay
section: The four cycles revisited
text:
The four cycles revisited
Giovanni Arrighi’s The Long Twentieth Century (1994) proposed that the history of capitalism can be read as a succession of systemic cycles of accumulation, each centred on a state-capital alliance that organises world commerce and finance during its ascendancy phase before entering its financial expansion phase and eventually yielding to a new challenger.
The Genoese cycle (15th-16th centuries) demonstrated that financial capitalism, the ability to control capital flows without territorial dominance, can generate disproportionate returns for those who hold the nodes through which capital must pass. The Genoese bankers financed Spanish and Portuguese empires without governing territories of their own, capturing a rent on the capital circuits of the Iberian world-economy. Their lesson: the most powerful position in a capitalist system is not ownership of production but control of the financial infrastructure through which production is financed.
The Dutch cycle (17th century) added institutional innovation to financial sophistication: the VOC, the Amsterdam Bourse, the Bank of Amsterdam, the Treaty of Westphalia. The Dutch invented the organisational forms, joint-stock companies, secondary markets, stable reserve currency, that all subsequent cycles would use. Their characteristic contribution was the institutionalisation of capitalism: creating the legal and financial architecture that makes capital accumulation scalable and transferable across time and space.
The British cycle (18th-19th centuries) added industrial production and free trade ideology to the financial and institutional innovations of predecessors. Britain’s productive supremacy in textiles, steel, and engineering provided the material foundation for its financial dominance (the gold-backed pound sterling as world reserve currency) and its ideological dominance (free trade as the universal prescription, implemented after Britain’s industrial supremacy was secure enough to benefit from open markets).
The American cycle (20th-21st centuries) added mass production, multilateral institution-building, and the dollar standard. The American cycle’s material expansion phase (1945-1970) was the most productive in capitalist history: reconstruction of Europe and Japan created new markets; Fordist mass production generated the wages that sustained mass consumption; the Bretton Woods system provided monetary stability; and the United Nations framework provided political legitimacy. The American cycle’s financial expansion phase (1970s onward) has progressively substituted financial engineering for productive investment, dollar printing for value creation, and regulatory arbitrage for genuine innovation.

title: 21  Chapter 19 — Hegemonic Cycles and the Long Run: A Concluding Essay
section: The signal crisis and its consequences
text:
The signal crisis and its consequences
Arrighi dates the signal crisis of the American cycle to 1971: Nixon’s closure of the gold window, which acknowledged that the United States could not maintain its Bretton Woods commitments without constraining the domestic monetary expansion that its political economy required. The subsequent fifty years have been the financial expansion phase of the American cycle: maintaining dollar dominance through financial mechanisms, Treasury bond recycling, dollar weaponisation, financial market innovation, rather than through productive supremacy.
The paradox of this phase: American financial dominance has been strengthened, not weakened, by the end of dollar-gold convertibility. Because no alternative exists as a store of value and medium of exchange for international trade, the world has continued accumulating dollar assets even as their gold backing disappeared and as the United States ran persistent current account deficits that would require balance-of-payments adjustment in any other economy. The “exorbitant privilege” analysed in Chapter 12 is the institutional expression of Arrighi’s M’-phase logic: the hegemon extracts systemic rents through its control of the monetary circuit rather than through the productivity of its production.
The terminal crisis of the American cycle is unfolding at irregular pace. 2008 was a signal of terminal crisis dynamics: the leading financial complex itself generated the global crisis, inverting the hegemon’s traditional role as systemic stabiliser. The 2016-2020 American withdrawal from multilateralism, rejecting the rules-based international order that the United States had constructed, is further evidence of a hegemon less willing to provide the public goods that its hegemony required. The China-United States technology conflict is the most direct expression of the hegemonic transition: a rising challenger whose productive and technological capacities now rival the incumbent in semiconductors, AI, electric vehicles, and renewable energy is meeting an incumbent that uses regulatory, financial, and military instruments to defend its position.

title: 21  Chapter 19 — Hegemonic Cycles and the Long Run: A Concluding Essay
section: The transition and its structural uncertainty
text:
The transition and its structural uncertainty
Every Arrighian hegemonic transition has involved a period of systemic chaos, Braudel’s term for the interregnum between the decline of one hegemonic order and the consolidation of the next. The period from the signal crisis to the terminal crisis can span decades, during which old institutions lose legitimacy without being replaced, geopolitical competition intensifies, and the rules of the international economic game become contested rather than settled.
Morocco has lived through one hegemonic transition already: the shift from British to American hegemony, through which the Protectorate was eventually ended as American post-war anti-colonialism replaced British imperial legitimacy. The current transition, from American unipolarity toward multipolarity, creates a different but analogous opportunity structure for a middle power positioned at the intersection of multiple great power spheres of influence.
The specific opportunity of systemic transitions for middle powers: during stable hegemonic periods, the rules are fixed and smaller actors adapt to them. During transitions, rules are contested, new institutions are being built, and actors with genuine assets and credible governance can negotiate terms of engagement rather than simply accepting dictation. Morocco’s ability to engage simultaneously with European, Chinese, Gulf, and African partners, without full alignment with any, positions it to extract value from the transition’s multi-directional character that would not be available in a stable hegemonic environment.

title: 21  Chapter 19 — Hegemonic Cycles and the Long Run: A Concluding Essay
section: Morocco in the hegemonic cycles: three moments of integration
text:
Morocco in the hegemonic cycles: three moments of integration
Morocco’s integration into the capitalist world-economy has occurred through three structurally distinct moments, each conditioned by the phase of the hegemonic cycle in which it occurred and each leaving structural residues that shape the possibilities available today.
The first moment (1830-1912) coincided with the late phase of the British cycle, its financialisation period. European commercial capital, seeking new accumulation frontiers as European domestic markets saturated, extended credit, extracted tariff concessions through unequal treaties, and established commercial networks across the Mediterranean periphery. Morocco’s fiscal dependence on European loans (particularly the 1904 loans that directly preceded the Protectorate) illustrates the structural dynamic: debt creates the leverage that converts economic presence into political control. The Treaty of Fez was not primarily a military conquest, it was the culmination of a fiscal dependency mechanism that the British cycle’s financial expansion phase constructed across its periphery.
The second moment (1912-1956) coincided with the American cycle’s ascent and the British cycle’s terminal crisis. The Protectorate restructured Morocco’s productive geography to serve French metropolitan accumulation: phosphate extraction, commercial agriculture on the Atlantic plains, minimal industrial development. The Maroc utile distinction was not a geographic discovery but a political allocation of infrastructure that concentrated accumulation potential in the Atlantic corridor and simultaneously converted interior Morocco into a labour reservoir. This spatial economy was rational from the perspective of French metropolitan capital in the American cycle’s material expansion phase, which was rebuilding Europe’s industrial capacity and needed raw materials and labour.
The third moment (1956-present) coincides with the American cycle’s late financial expansion phase. The Volcker shock’s transfer of adjustment costs to peripheral debtors directly produced Morocco’s 1983 Structural Adjustment Programme. The subsequent insertion into European automotive and aerospace value chains occurred during the phase when European firms were reorganising their supply chains toward lower-cost adjacent locations, a strategy that served European capital’s need to respond to Asian competition by accessing lower-wage assembly capacity without the logistical or regulatory complexity of far-shore operations.
In Arrighi’s framework, each of Morocco’s integration moments was shaped by the hegemonic cycle’s dynamics at least as much as by Morocco’s autonomous choices. But each moment also created structural capabilities that the next moment could build on: the agricultural infrastructure of the Protectorate became the basis for the Plan Maroc Vert’s modern agricultural strategy; the phosphate industry nationalised in 1975 became OCP’s platform for the fertiliser upgrading that is now extending toward battery materials; the automotive cluster inserted in European value chains is now the industrial base from which EV component development is possible.
This reading suggests a structural optimism that is not naive: Morocco’s development is constrained by the structural dynamics of the hegemonic cycle in which it operates, but not determined by them. Each constraint creates pressure that, if creatively engaged rather than passively absorbed, generates new capabilities. The SAP’s destruction of Morocco’s directed credit instruments was a genuine loss of industrial policy capacity, and it generated the political and administrative learning that made Morocco a more sophisticated interlocutor with international financial institutions in subsequent decades. The automotive cluster’s current assembly-without-deepening limitation is simultaneously a demonstration that Morocco can attract world-class manufacturing investment and a specification of what the next phase of industrial policy must address.
